# Education in Finland
Finnish education places a high emphasis on early childhood development, viewing it as a critical stage for lifelong learning. This preparatory period, which lasts until age seven, is characterized by a philosophy centered on respect for individuality, encouraging social and interactive skills, and learning through play, rather than formal instruction in reading and mathematics. Finland has provided free universal daycare for children aged eight months to five years since 1990, and a year of preschool/kindergarten at age six since 1996.
The compulsory educational system is structured around a nine-year comprehensive school (grades 1 to 9). Following this, education becomes compulsory until age 18 and bifurcates into academic tracks (Lukio) or vocational tracks (Ammattioppilaitos) at the upper secondary and tertiary levels. Both tracks are free, and students are entitled to school healthcare, free meals, and materials. The system is non-selective, as private schools are prohibited from charging tuition or admitting students based on selection criteria, ensuring equal access for all. Teachers are highly qualified, holding a master's degree, and enjoy significant autonomy in teaching methods.
